sounds.intro: Sanskrit's sounds are known unusually well. Ancient phoneticians, the authors of the Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣās and the grammarian Pāṇini, described where and how each sound is made, and the alphabet itself is ordered by their descriptions. Recitation has never stopped either, though it has picked up regional accents. This guide gives the Classical sounds as the grammarians describe them, with notes where modern practice differs.

rows.like: short and dull, like the u in 'cup'
rows.note: Pāṇini and two Prātiśākhyas call short a 'covered': it is not simply a short ā.

rows.like: a in 'father', held for two beats
short i as in 'bit' but tenser; long ī as in 'machine'
short u as in 'put'; long ū as in 'rule'
an untrilled r that makes a syllable by itself, close to the vowel of American 'bird'
rows.note: Most of North India now says ri (Krishna); Marathi and Gujarati speakers, and the Telugu country, say ru (Krushna).

rows.like: an l used as a vowel, as in 'bottle'
rows.note: Found only in forms of one root, kḷp 'be fit'.

rows.like: e in 'they' and o in 'go', held steady without a glide
rows.note: Always long. They were once the diphthongs ai and au, which is why a + i fuse into e.

rows.like: as in 'aisle' and 'how'
velar: the back of the tongue against the soft palate; ṅ is the ng of 'sing'
palatal: the tongue pressed flat on the hard palate; ñ is the ny of 'canyon'
rows.note: Most reciters today say c and j as in 'church' and 'judge'.

rows.like: retroflex: the tongue tip curled back to the roof of the mouth
dental: the tongue tip against the upper teeth, further forward than English t
labial: made with the lips
no puff of breath at all, like the k, t and p in 'skin', 'stop' and 'spin'
a strong puff, as in 'kin', 'top' and 'pin' said firmly. ph is never f, and th is never as in 'thin'
plain voiced sounds, as in English
voiced, with a breathy release, like the g-h in 'doghouse' or the d-h in 'redhead' run into one sound

groups.h: Retroflex sounds and the three s's

rows.like: t and d with the tongue tip curled up and back. To Indian ears these, not the dental t and d, sound like English t and d
n with the tongue tip curled back
sh with the tongue tip curled back
rows.note: Many speakers today make no difference between ṣ and ś.

rows.like: sh as in 'sheep', with the tongue raised flat toward the palate
s as in 'sun', never z
a curled-back l, which the Ṛgveda writes for ḍ between vowels
rows.note: As in agnim īḷe, the first words of the Ṛgveda.

rows.like: y as in 'yes'
a light tap of the tongue, as in Spanish 'pero'
a clear l, as in 'leaf'
between English v and w. The old phoneticians made it with the lower lip against the upper teeth
rows.note: After a consonant, as in tvam, it often sounds closer to w.

rows.like: a voiced, breathy h
the vowel carried on through the nose. Before a stop it is said as that row's nasal, so saṃbhavāmi sounds like sambhavāmi
rows.note: Before y, r, l, v, ś, ṣ, s and h the old texts describe a nasal vowel; today it is often said as m or ng.

rows.like: a voiceless h breathed out after the vowel
rows.note: Reciters today often add a faint echo of the vowel: naraḥ sounds like nara-ha, agniḥ like agni-hi.

tips.p: Dictionaries follow the phonetic order of the varṇamālā: the vowels a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ e ai o au, then ṃ and ḥ, then the stops row by row from the back of the mouth to the lips (the k, c, ṭ, t and p rows), then y r l v, then ś ṣ s h. Each row runs voiceless, voiceless with breath, voiced, voiced with breath, nasal: k kh g gh ṅ. So kh is a letter of its own, filed after every word in k.

A short vowel lasts one beat (mātrā) and a long one two. Length changes meaning, as in bala 'strength' and bāla 'boy', and it drives the rhythm of verse (unit 12). e and o are always long, and ai and au count as long.

tips.h: Breath is part of the letter
tips.p: kara 'hand' and khara 'hard' differ only in the puff after k. Voiced aspirates like gh, dh and bh are the hardest for English speakers: say the consonant and let a breathy h follow at once, with no vowel in between.
Classical texts were written without accent marks, and the grammarians describe only pitch, never stress. Give long and heavy syllables their full length and the rhythm comes by itself.

The Vedas had a pitch accent: a raised syllable (udātta), unraised ones (anudātta) and a falling tone (svarita). Vedic manuscripts mark it and priests still chant it, but Classical Sanskrit lost it. The Ṛgveda also writes ḷ (ळ) for ḍ between vowels, and some old phoneticians describe special breaths before k and p (jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya).

Sanskrit is still recited all over India, coloured by local languages, so there is no single modern standard. Short a sounds like the u in 'cup', and a final a is always said (Rāma, never 'Ram'). ṛ becomes ri or ru, jñ is said gy in the north and dny in Maharashtra, and ṣ often merges with ś. The audio here uses a Hindi voice, so it follows northern habits and may drop a final a that Sanskrit keeps.

grammar.title: Pronouns: I, we, you
grammar.note: These pronouns have no gender. The short forms in brackets never begin a sentence; te is the 'to you' in namaste. The dual (āvām 'we two', yuvām 'you two') is left out.
